newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Rubber - Weak demand, ample output keeps prices soft.
newsitem.headline: Rubber - Weak demand, ample output keeps prices soft.

text.p: After a recent bout of modest shortcovering, soft consumer demand and rising production will probably drag Southeast Asian rubber prices lower this week, regional dealers said on Monday.
"The market still looks no good and I don't expect it to get better. Demand is weak and production is moving up," a dealer for a rubber commodity house in Singapore said.
"I think we'll see a half-cent to one-cent fall across the board daily," a dealer in Malaysia added.
Traders said the recent hot and dry weather in most rubber-producing countries has helped raise production as this facilitated the tapping of rubber trees.
"The dry weather is helping the rubber. We heard from producers that their output has been moving up," a dealer said.
Regional traders were also sceptical that the intervention of Bangkok, which is spending one billion baht to prop up Thai rubber prices, would give the market a permanent lift.
"What is the Thai government going to do with all that rubber? Who are they going to sell it to when we traders ourselves have problems? That we'd like to know," a dealer in Kuala Lumpur said.

But Thai dealers were hopeful the intervention scheme will help support prices in the market. They welcomed a remark by an industry official that the Thai government will not sell the rubber it has accumulated until world prices improved.
"It is good to know that it will not spend all the four billion baht to prop up prices. The government intervention helps in the way that it drains out excess supply," a dealer in Thailand said.
"But at the same time it forces us to buy at high prices while world (rubber) prices are bearish," the trader conceded.
A dealer in Singapore said the absence of solid offtake from China was also weighing on regional trade. "Some buying by China would definitely help," the dealer said.

"China's idea of prices was much lower than what is quoted in the market now. I don't think heavy buying interest from that country will emerge at this level," a dealer in the Thai rubber centre of Hat Yai said.
Other traders said China is likely to keep a low profile in the market because it has ample stocks of rubber.
"On the top of that, it is more difficult to get a letter of credit for rubber these days in China. One has to put 30-50 percent deposit up front," a Bangkok-based dealer said.
The Thai benchmark RSS3 was quoted at around 116.00 U.S. cents a kg for August shipment and 117.00 US cents a kg for September shipment.
The Malaysian Rubber Exchange and Licensing Board (MRELB) quoted July buyer for the benchmark RSS1 at 284 Malaysian cents a kg at the close of trade on Friday, down one cent from the previous week.

July SMR20 buyer was quoted at 263 cents, down three cents from the previous week. Dealers quoted SMR 20 at 260 cents a kg, SMR CV at 331 cents, SMR L at 308 cents, SMR 10 at 262 cents and drum latex at 226 cents.
In Indonesia, traders said they expected prices of the benchmark SIR20 rubber to soften further this week after several deals were concluded in Palembang.
"We expect prices to soften this week because the market seemed to lose direction after the Palembang deal," one said.
"Some traders think that falls in Tokyo contributed to the poor sentiment in Indonesia," said another trader.
Traders said a deal was done at 47.50 U.S. cents/lb FOB Palembang, lower than Thursday's level of 48.00 cents. No buying interest was reported in other centres in the country.
Offer prices were quoted at 48.25 cents FOB Medan, 47.75 cents FOB Padang and Surabaya and at 47.25 cents FOB Pontianak and Jambi, dealers said.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
